title: I am…
titleJp: わたしは がくせいです
canDo: I can say who I am: my name, my nationality and what I do (student, teacher…).
I can turn a statement into a yes/no question and answer it.

I can link two nouns: "a student at university X", "a Japanese teacher", "my name".

Recognizing basic katakana helps with names and countries (アメリカ, マリア), but it is not required: the kana reading is always shown.

what (the form used before です)

grammar.title: X は Y です
grammar.explanation:
The most basic Japanese sentence: it says what X is. **は marks the topic** — what the sentence is about ("as for X…"). As a particle, は is read **wa**, not "ha". **です always comes at the end** and means "is / am / are" in the polite style.
• です never changes with the person or number: I am, you are, they are — all です.
• There are no articles and no plural: がくせい can be "a student", "the student" or "students".
• When the topic is obvious, it disappears: introducing yourself, just ブラジルじんです。 is enough — repeating わたしは in every sentence sounds robotic.

examples.jp: わたしは ブラジルじんです。
examples.kana: わたしは ブラジルじんです。
examples.en: I'm Brazilian. [lit. as for me, Brazilian is]

examples.jp: たなかさんは せんせいです。
examples.kana: たなかさんは せんせいです。

examples.jp: ジョンさんは だいがくせいです。
examples.kana: ジョンさんは だいがくせいです。

pitfalls: は as a particle is read "wa" — but inside a word it stays "ha": はい (hai), はな (hana).
Never put さん after your own name: わたしは ジョンさんです ✗ → わたしは ジョンです ✓.
です is not "is located": to say where something is, Japanese uses a different verb (lesson 04-1). がっこうは です ✗ — です needs the Y (what X is).
howToStudy: Say 5 true sentences about yourself out loud, changing only Y: ブラジルじんです → がくせいです → …
Tap 🔬 on the examples: the block with は is the TOPIC, the block with です is the PREDICATE — always read starting from the predicate.
In your notebook, write 3 sentences about people you know (〜さんは 〜です).

grammar.title: 〜か (questions)
grammar.explanation:
To ask a question, just put **か at the end**. The word order does **not** change — Japanese never inverts like English "Are you…?". In speech your voice rises on か; in formal writing the sentence ends with 。, because か already does the job of the question mark.
• A "yes" answer: はい、そうです。 ("Yes, that's right.")
• A "no" answer, for now: いいえ + the correct information (いいえ、アメリカじんです。). The full negative form comes in lesson 02-3.
• With a question word, the question word goes **exactly where the answer will go**: せんこうは なんですか。 → せんこうは れきしです。 Before です, "what" is なん.
grammar.structure: [X] は [Y] ですか。 · [X] は なんですか。

examples.jp: せんせいですか。— はい、そうです。
examples.kana: せんせいですか。— はい、そうです。
examples.romaji: Sensei desu ka. — Hai, sō desu.
examples.en: Are you a teacher? — Yes, I am.

examples.jp: マリアさんは にほんじんですか。— いいえ、ブラジルじんです。
examples.kana: マリアさんは にほんじんですか。— いいえ、ブラジルじんです。
examples.romaji: Maria-san wa nihonjin desu ka. — Iie, burajirujin desu.
examples.en: Is Maria Japanese? — No, she's Brazilian.

examples.jp: せんこうは なんですか。— けいざいです。
examples.kana: せんこうは なんですか。— けいざいです。
examples.romaji: Senkō wa nan desu ka. — Keizai desu.

pitfalls: Don't reorder the sentence to ask: take the statement and add か. ですか がくせい ✗ → がくせいですか ✓.
"What" before です is なん (なんですか), not なに: なにですか ✗ → なんですか ✓.
Japanese usually avoids saying "you" (あなた) — calling someone あなた can sound cold. Use their name + さん, or no subject at all.
howToStudy: Take the 5 sentences you said in the previous point and turn each into a question; answer はい、そうです to each.
Ask 3 questions with なんですか about things you can answer (せんこうは なんですか…).
When you hear dialogues in the video, notice how the voice rises on か.

grammar.title: N₁ の N₂
grammar.explanation:
の links two nouns: the **first describes the second**, and the second is the core — the thing you are talking about. The order is like English "'s" (John's book = ジョンさんの ほん), and the reverse of "of" (teacher of Japanese = にほんごの せんせい).
• Possession: わたしの なまえ ("my name"). "My", "your", "his" are just person + の.
• Belonging: サンパウロだいがくの がくせい ("a student at the University of São Paulo").
• Subject/field: にほんごの せんせい ("a Japanese teacher").
• It chains: わたしの だいがくの せんせい ("a teacher at my university").
grammar.structure: [N₁] の [N₂] — N₂ is the main thing

examples.jp: わたしの なまえは マリアです。
examples.kana: わたしの なまえは マリアです。
examples.romaji: Watashi no namae wa Maria desu.

examples.jp: ペドロさんは サンパウロだいがくの がくせいです。
examples.kana: ペドロさんは サンパウロだいがくの がくせいです。
examples.romaji: Pedoro-san wa Sanpauro daigaku no gakusei desu.
examples.en: Pedro is a student at the University of São Paulo.

examples.jp: にほんごの せんせいは たなかさんです。
examples.kana: にほんごの せんせいは たなかさんです。
examples.romaji: Nihongo no sensei wa Tanaka-san desu.
examples.en: The Japanese teacher is Mr./Ms. Tanaka.

pitfalls: Swapping the order changes the meaning: せんせいの にほんご is "the teacher's Japanese", not "the Japanese teacher".
This の links noun to noun. Adjectives attach differently, without の (lesson 05-1): たかいの やま ✗ → たかい やま ✓.
Don't translate every English "of/from/by" with の: "go by bus" or "leave from home" use other particles (lessons 03-2 and 10-3). の is only for noun + noun.
howToStudy: Translate out loud: "the teacher's name" → せんせいの なまえ; "a history student" → れきしの がくせい.
Tap 🔬 on the Pedro example: サンパウロだいがくの shows up as DESCRIBES NEXT, attached to がくせい.
Write 3 things of yours in your notebook with わたしの… (なまえ, せんこう, だいがく).

culture.title: Bowing (おじぎ)
culture.body: In Japan, introductions come with a **bow**, not a handshake or a kiss on the cheek. Among colleagues, a slight bow of about 15° (会釈 eshaku) is enough: back straight, eyes lowering naturally. Deeper bows (around 30° and 45°) show more respect or a serious apology. With foreigners, many Japanese people offer a hand — return a light handshake with a small nod. A bow usually goes with はじめまして。…よろしく おねがいします。, which you saw in lesson 00-3.
culture.try: In front of a mirror, say はじめまして。わたしは (your name) です。よろしく おねがいします。 and do an 会釈 on よろしく.

I can build N₁ の N₂ in the right order (a Japanese teacher = にほんごの せんせい).
